'Is the antiparticle of' is not functional: a particle can be the antiparticle of more than one particle. (edit)
So being the antiparticle of the electron no longer rules out being the antiparticle of the proton: yes, it can.

notes: RBox edit that removes a functional property that holds: every particle has exactly one antiparticle (some, like the photon, are their own), so a particle is the antiparticle of at most one particle; there is no real exception (whether neutrinos are Majorana particles only decides whether a neutrino is its own antiparticle, still one; K-short and K-long are mixtures of the kaon and antikaon, each still with one CPT conjugate). The instance facts are real (the positron is the antiparticle of the electron; the antiproton that of the proton), so before the edit the second value is ruled out (no), after it it no longer is ('can' = not ruled out: yes). The second instance uses the neutron, whose antiparticle is the antineutron. Round-2 verifier: questions rephrased from 'Does it follow that ... is not ...?' to 'Can ... also ...?' (new answer yes) to keep the topic's RBox yes/no balance after 0017 became a removal; near query rephrased to match (mirror nucleus: no). Chinese 正电子 is the standard name for the positron and does not give the answer away.
